The Senior Editor of The Philadelphia Daily News Wins The March Reefer Madness Prize

(Marijuananews note: I have decided to give a monthly Reefer Madness prize to deserving journalists. My criteria are purely subjective, which seems only fair. This month’s prize goes to an old friend, whom I have not seen since the early 60s -- when marijuana was definitely not our drug of choice.

I was at Yale with Russ Byers, and he is, well, smart enough to know better....

This piece contradicts itself, which is why I like it so much. I agree with it half the time!

Remember, this is in the city where the Class Action lawsuit is taking place, and the Daily News’s sister paper, the Inquirer, has had some excellent articles.)

SURVEY: KIDS 13 ARE DRUG-SMART

From The Philadelphia Daily News
Dailynews.opinion@phillynews.com
http://interactive.phillynews.com/talk-show/
http://www.phillynews.com/

March 30, 1999

By W. Russell G. Byers, Daily News columnist (W. Russell G. Byers is senior editor of the Daily News. Send e-mail to russell.byers@phillynews.com)

The rush is on to portray pot as just another recreational drug that may actually have some desirable medicinal value.

Even the prestigious Institute of Medicine of the National Academy of Science seems to have joined the pro-pot parade.

(Marijuananews note: Philadelphia has a great museum for the works of the sculptor, Rodin. The entrance features his famous "Gates of Hell." I don’t recall if any of the figures were teens smoking joints. The fact is that,  while kids should not be smoking marijuana, the overwhelming majority do not have serious problems as the result of using it.)

Armed with multiple studies proving just that point, Joe Califano, president of the National Center on Addiction and Substance Abuse (CASA) at Columbia University, pleads with parents, teachers and principals to watch for drug use among even 12- and 13-year-olds. A 1998 CASA survey (see chart) shows kids "growing up" in that one pivotal year in ways that ought to scare the dickens out of everyone.
(Marijuananews note: That is the year that most kids go from elementary to middle schools, so it should not be surprising that they learn new things, good and bad. It isn’t long before they learn that they have been lied to about marijuana and make the mistake of thinking that they have been lied to about everything else. Unfortunately, it is also the time when they experiment most with inhalants, truly the most dangerous psychoactive substances. But no mention of that here.)

The vast majority of 12-year-olds are pretty innocent about drugs. One year later, however, 40 and 50 percent can buy pot, LSD, cocaine or heroin and know a teen who uses acid, cocaine or heroin. And almost half the 13-year-olds in the survey would not report a student they see using illegal drugs.
(Marijuananews note: Marijuana prohibition is certainly working well, isn’t it?)

Drugs are, quite obviously, ubiquitous. But teachers and principals in high school seem oblivious to their effects.

Asked by CASA if they could "use marijuana every weekend and still do well in school," only 23 percent of high-schoolers said yes.

Yet half of their teachers and principals felt such consistent marijuana use wouldn’t affect their students’ performance.

Maybe those teachers, and even some members of the press, are in denial about marijuana today because nothing about drug use, today, compares to what it was 10, 20 and 30 years ago.

To begin with, today’s pot is 10, 20 and even 30 times more powerful than it used to be. Decades ago, you had to work to get high. Today, you have to work to avoid it.

(Marijuananews note: This is really ridiculous. Did Joe Califano tell Byers that? First, there is no data from 30 years ago. Second, according to DEAland government statistics, 20 years ago average THC content was around 2% THC, and according to NIDA the average today is around 3% on a weight adjusted basis. That is, the average on the market is around 3%. There was above average marijuana available 20 or 30 years ago, just as there is today. That is how you get averages, unless it is all the same. The chances of a teen getting the best – or worst, if you prefer – is about the same as his getting drunk on Dom Perignon champagne. Only in the best -- or worst, if you prefer – of families.)

See
Marijuana Prohibition And Potency, Price, And Safety -- 
"Is Marijuana Stronger Than It Was Back In the '60s, When Everyone Thought It Was Harmless?"
Analysis By Richard Cowan

Decades ago, even if you got high on marijuana, that was it because marijuana was the only drug readily available.
(Marijuananews note: Oh come on! There was no LSD in the 60s? No cocaine in the 70s? Rent a tape of Superfly)
Today, as CASA’s survey of 13-year-olds makes clear, marijuana is a gateway to LSD, cocaine or heroin.
(Marijuananews note: Even the "Gateway Theory" does not claim that most kids who use marijuana use hard drugs.  Rather, it simply argues -- correctly -- that few people ever use hard drugs without using marijuana first. From that, they illogically conclude that eliminating marijuana use would reduce hard drug use. I think that it would have the opposite effect.)

See
The Wall Street Journal Responds To The IOM Report
By Having Califano Defend The "Gateway Theory"
and
What If Marijuana Disappeared? By Richard Cowan
Although you probably haven’t seen it in press reports, Califano reminds us that even the medical institute’s researchers seem to agree on this key point. "Marijuana serves as a gateway," the report says, "to the world of illegal drugs in which youths have greater opportunity and are under greater social pressure to try other illegal drugs."

(Marijuananews note: Yes, and even former National Directors of NORML, editors of Marijuananews and evil legalizers, all agree that illegal "marijuana serves as a gateway to the world of illegal drugs in which youths have greater opportunity and are under greater social pressure to try other illegal drugs." But why doesn't that happen with beer? Because beer is not sold in "the world of illegal drugs.")

See
"Here, if you want cannabis you go to a coffee shop.
In other countries if you want it you have to go to a man who might try to sell you heroin or cocaine as well."

Yes, it does have valid medicinal use. Decades ago, I saw it used (illegally) by a neighbor who was suffering from terminal breast cancer. Her son smuggled her two joints a night because they were the best way for her to get a peaceful sleep in her final months.

But for teens and pre-teens, it’s a gateway almost straight to hell. Instead of sending them a mixed message about its potential medicinal value, the Institute of Medicine should simply tell them Pot’s Not Hot.

(Marijuananews note: Excuse me! I hate to point this out, but this column just sent a "mixed message about its potential medicinal value." He admits twice that is has medical value. But the real questions are --
Should his friend and the mother dying of cancer have been arrested?
Should his friend have let his mother die in agony?

The IOM was charged with determining whether marijuana has medical value. They agreed with Byers that it does. They also addressed his concerns and concluded that medical access should not have any major impact on teen marijuana use.

According to Byers’s own numbers, while marijuana prohibition is keeping the sick and dying from getting the help his friend's mother received, it doesn’t seem to have reduced its availability to 13-yearolds.)
